summary: Inspired by the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" and driven by the thousands of pounds of equipment left in space, our team aims to bridge the gap between the history of these machines and school-aged children. This NASA machinery has left its mark on the history of space exploration, yet many of them, such as Surveyor 3 or Viking 1 remain mostly unknown to the general audience, especially amongst youngsters. Thus, our team developed an interactive online 3D game (with a target audience of 7-11 year olds, but anyone is welcome to test it!), which features a map of the Moon, Mars as well as Deep Space. The user may wander around the map and explore abandoned equipment along, accompanied by a short description about their mission that is also available to listen. It also features a quiz to check your answers at the end. Why don’t you go ahead and give it a try?
details:
Space Riders is a free 3D browser adventure for children aged 7 to 11. Young learners explore the Moon, Mars and deep space, in which they will find the riders that NASA left behind after their missions concluded. Examples include the Apollo 17 Rover, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking 1 and Ingenuity. Each find opens a picture and a short story. After finding every rider, the user returns to their spaceship and earns a downloadable “Space Explorer” certificate. There is also a 10-question quiz at the end.

The project works with an HTML file that runs with no install or login. three.js renders the 3D worlds and checks the student's distance to each ghost’s beacon. Browser APIs handle the speech synthesis for a narrator, canvas creates the certificate and the gyroscope makes the VR look-around on phones.

It also makes little-known NASA history approachable and teaches real facts by play. It is accessible, free and private, with narration and large buttons included. We hope to give users of all ages, especially children, a fun starting point to learn more about the machinery that humans have left behind.

We used HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, three.js (WebGL), DeviceOrientation APIs, NASA imagery and NSSDCA. It is currently hosted in GitHub Pages.
